Bio-Engineering the Future

Introduction to Biotechnology and Recombinant DNA Tools

screens.title: A Life-Saving Code
screens.html:
🔑

A Life-Saving Code

Imagine living with a condition where your body cannot produce a vital protein, like insulin.

Before 1978, insulin was harvested from the pancreases of cows and pigs. Today, we use 'biological factories' to grow human insulin.

How do we teach a bacterium to build a human hormone?

Key point

Biotechnology involves using biological systems, organisms, or derivatives to develop products for human health.

screens.title: Knowledge Audit: DNA Structure
screens.html:
QUICK REVIEW

Knowledge Audit: DNA Structure

To manipulate DNA, we must understand its architecture. DNA is a polymer of nucleotides, each consisting of a phosphate group, a deoxyribose sugar, and a nitrogenous base.

Complementary Base Pairing

Adenine (A) pairs with Thymine (T)

Cytosine (C) pairs with Guanine (G)

The strands are anti-parallel (5' to 3').

screens.title: The Genetic Toolbelt
screens.html:
The Genetic Toolbelt

Genetic engineering uses tools to cut, paste, copy, and view DNA, often adapted from natural biological processes.

Restriction Enzymes - Molecular scissors cutting DNA at specific sequences.

DNA Ligase - Molecular glue joining DNA fragments together.

Vectors - Vehicles transporting foreign DNA into host cells.

screens.title: KEY CONCEPT
screens.html:
KEY CONCEPT

Restriction Enzymes: Molecular Scissors

Restriction endonucleases (enzymes) occur naturally in bacteria as a defence mechanism against viral DNA.

They recognise a specific sequence of nucleotides called a recognition site (usually 4–8 base pairs long) and cut the phosphodiester backbone of the DNA.

screens.title: Sticky Ends vs Blunt Ends
screens.html:
Sticky Ends vs Blunt Ends

Enzymes create two DNA end types, determining how easily fragments are joined.

Sticky Ends

Staggered cuts leave overhangs that bond easily with complementary sequences.

Blunt Ends

A straight cut through both strands. These lack overhangs and are harder to rejoin.

screens.title: DNA Ligase: The Glue
screens.html:
🧠

DNA Ligase: The Glue

While hydrogen bonds may hold 'sticky' ends together temporarily, they aren't permanent.

DNA Ligase is the enzyme that creates solid phosphodiester bonds between the sugar-phosphate backbones of two DNA fragments, making them one continuous strand.

Remember

Ligase is essential for repair and replication in cells, but in the lab, we use it to create Recombinant DNA.

screens.title: Why must we use the same enzyme for both genes?
screens.html:
Why must we use the same enzyme for both genes?

Think about the shape of the 'sticky ends'. If you cut the human insulin gene with Enzyme A and the bacterial plasmid with Enzyme B, would they fit together?

screens.title: Vectors and Plasmids
screens.html:
Vectors and Plasmids

To get our human DNA into a cell, we need a vector. In human biology applications, we often use plasmids—small, circular loops of extra-chromosomal DNA found in bacteria.

1

Plasmids are cut with a restriction enzyme.

2

The target gene is inserted into the gap.

3

The plasmid is taken up by a bacterial host.

screens.title: KEY CONCEPT
screens.html:
KEY CONCEPT

PCR: The Molecular Photocopy

The Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) is a technique used to amplify a specific sequence of DNA, creating millions of copies from a tiny sample.

This is vital for forensics, diagnostics, and genetic testing when the initial sample is too small.

screens.title: The Three Stages of PCR
screens.html:
The Three Stages of PCR

Denaturation (95°C)

Heat is used to break hydrogen bonds, separating the double-stranded DNA into two single strands.

Annealing (55°C)

Primers (short DNA sequences) bind to the complementary sequences at the ends of the target DNA.

Extension (72°C)

Taq Polymerase synthesises new DNA strands by adding nucleotides starting from the primers.

screens.title: Why Taq Polymerase?
screens.html:
🤯

Why Taq Polymerase?

Human DNA polymerase would denature (break down) at the 95°C required for PCR.

Instead, we use DNA polymerase from Thermus aquaticus, a bacterium that lives in hot springs. Its enzymes are thermostable.

Fun fact

Taq polymerase was discovered in Yellowstone National Park's geothermal pools!

screens.title: Gel Electrophoresis
screens.html:
Gel Electrophoresis

Once we have cut DNA or amplified it, we need to see what we've got.

Gel Electrophoresis separates DNA fragments based on their size and electrical charge.

DNA is negatively charged.

It moves through an agarose gel towards the positive electrode.

screens.title: How the Gel Works
screens.html:
🧠

How the Gel Works

The agarose gel acts like a sieve. Shorter fragments of DNA can wiggle through the pores more easily than long fragments.

Remember

Smaller fragments travel further; larger fragments stay closer to the wells.

screens.title: The DNA Ladder
screens.html:
The DNA Ladder

How do we know the actual size of our fragments? We use a DNA ladder (or marker).

This is a solution with DNA fragments of known lengths (e.g., 100bp, 500bp, 1000bp). By comparing our sample bands to the ladder, we can estimate their size.

screens.title: Combining the Tools
screens.html:
Combining the Tools

In professional biotechnology, these tools are never used in isolation. We use PCR to amplify a gene, restriction enzymes to cut it out, gel electrophoresis to verify the size, and then ligase to insert it into a vector.

screens.title: HUMAN HEALTH
screens.html:
HUMAN HEALTH

🔍

Application: Helping Diabetics

Recombinant DNA (rDNA) technology has revolutionised the treatment of Type 1 Diabetes. By inserting the human insulin gene into E. coli bacteria, we produce mass quantities of pure human insulin.

Example

This prevents allergic reactions that sometimes occurred when using animal-derived insulin.

PCR increases the total amount of DNA in a tube but does not change the genetic sequence.

👍​

b) PCR is a replication technique that uses Taq polymerase to build exact copies of the template DNA sequence.

screens.title: Introduction to Gene Therapy
screens.html:
Introduction to Gene Therapy

Beyond making hormones, biotechnology aims to 'fix' faulty genes inside the human body. This is Gene Therapy.

Instead of making a protein in a lab and injecting it, we use vectors (like modified viruses) to deliver healthy genes directly into the patient's cells.

screens.title: Future Frontiers
screens.html:
🔑

Future Frontiers

As we progress through this unit, we will look at how these tools create vaccines, treat thyroid disorders, and even hold the potential to treat Alzheimer's through cell replacement therapy.

Key point

Precision is the goal. The better our tools, the fewer side effects for patients.

screens.title: Critical Thinking: The Cost of Progress
screens.html:
Critical Thinking: The Cost of Progress

If biotech allows us to produce any human protein, should we limit engineering? Consider the difference between treating disease and enhancing human traits.

screens.title: Critical Thinking: The Cost of Progress
screens.html:
Critical Thinking: The Cost of Progress

You might have said...

Treating disease is a medical necessity to improve quality of life.

Enhancement risks social inequality and eugenics.

Expensive biotech may divide the 'enhanced' and 'un-enhanced'.

Long-term genetic consequences of changing human biology are unknown.

✅​

screens.title: Mastering the Basics
screens.html:
Mastering the Basics

Today we've mastered the 'alphabet' of biotechnology. Next time, we will apply these tools to see how they are used to build specific hormones and vaccines for the Western Australian healthcare system.

questions.title: Written practice
questions.prompt: Explain how restriction enzymes and DNA ligase are used to construct a recombinant plasmid.
steps: Cut the plasmid and the desired DNA using suitable restriction enzymes to produce compatible ends.
Allow complementary ends to pair and use DNA ligase to seal the DNA backbone.
The recombinant plasmid carries the inserted DNA and can be introduced into a suitable host cell.

bank.why: DNA ligase joins DNA fragments by forming bonds in the sugar–phosphate backbone.

bank.q: Why are plasmids useful as vectors?
o: They can carry inserted DNA into host cells
bank.why: Plasmids are small DNA molecules that can be used to carry inserted genes into a host.

bank.q: What does a restriction enzyme do?
o: Cuts DNA at particular recognition sequences
bank.why: Restriction enzymes recognise particular DNA sequences and cut DNA there.
